newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - Traders take stock as year-end approaches.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Traders take stock as year-end approaches.

text.p: Activity in U.S. spot refined products markets was expected to be relatively quiet early in the week as traders took stock of positions heading into the final month of the year, traders said on Monday.
But with the New Year fast approaching, year-end accounting demands will fuel active trading in the weeks before the markets turn less liquid ahead of the holidays, traders said.
Activity today was muted as key players recovered from the long Thanksgiving Day holiday weekend.
"Some people are still missing so we've got the holiday blahs. I don't see much being done," one New York Harbor products trader said.
Traders pegged New York heating oil differentials at about 0.20 cent above January futures, little changed from before the long Thanksgiving weekend which began on Thursday.

"Short-term, I think heating oil will be steady but there's still a little room to knock it around (lower) if it doesn't get colder," one trader said, noting the return of seasonal fall temperatures after last week's cold snap.
Smith Barney meteorologist Jon Davis said he sees normal temperatures for the U.S. Northeast and most of the United States for the next four or five days.
"And then it should trend cooler over the weekend but nothing exceptionally cold," he said.
Early Monday activity in New York Harbor remained very subdued, with many market players squaring their books and seeking to assess prices.
Gasoline activity may take center stage this week, one trader said, though few serious players emerged early Monday from the long holiday weekend to lend direction to prices.

The expiration of the December futures last week and the roll in the basis price to the January contract led to some hesitation early Monday. "It's very quiet and nobody knows what to do," one Northeast trader said.
While traders take steps to improve their year-end inventory positions, some said relatively low inventories would limit moves that can be made before the end of the year.
"I think you are going to have to make your moves this week or you may not be able to get them implemented," a Chicago-area trader said.
In the Midwest, differentials on late-month unleaded gasoline and diesel fuel remained well below first-cycle differentials on talk of late-month deliveries headed into the market.
The weaker differentials and general lack of liquidity in the final two weeks of the year should fuel active sessions late in the week, traders said.
"It's going to be quiet through the first half of the week, but once we get the (last-in, first-out accounting) numbers, things are going to start hopping," another Midwest trader said on Monday.
